newsitem.title: JAPAN: POLL-Japan c/a surplus unlikely to fall soon.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Japan c/a surplus unlikely to fall soon.

text.p: The surplus in Japan's current account, the broadest measure of goods and services trade, is likely to rise for the first time in five years this fiscal year, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Thursday.
Although most economists do not expect the surplus for the year as a whole to grow as significantly as it has in recent months, they do not see a turnaround in its rising trend.

Forecasts from 35 economists produced an average of 10.0 trillion yen for the current account surplus for this fiscal year, up from the 7.18 trillion yen surplus in the previous business year, which ended on March 31.
The survey was conducted from July 7 to July 9.
Behind the expected rise in the current account surplus was the growth in Japan's trade surplus, which has recently posted sharp rises on the back of strong exports, economists said.
"The trade surplus is growing. Japan's exports will continue to increase in the 1997/98 fiscal year," said Mamoru Yamaguchi, an economist at Nikko Research Center.

"The (trade) surplus will continue to rise gradually during the current fiscal year if the dollar/yen rate remains at the current level of around 112 to 113 yen to a dollar," added Yoshiteru Hoshi, an economist at DKB Research Institute.
The economists, on average, predicted that the trade surplus for this business year would hit 11.6 trillion yen, up from a surplus of 8.81 trillion yen the previous business year.
The Finance Ministry said earlier on Thursday that Japan posted a trade surplus of 934.21 billion yen in June, a rise of 27.7 percent from a year ago.
The economists said the stronger exports were brought about by the lingering effects of a weak yen earlier in May and by healthy economic growth overseas, especially in the United States.
Nikko's Yamaguchi also said weak domestic demand will continue to keep the trade surplus on a rising trend.

Domestic demand, mainly private consumption, dropped following a rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, leading to a decrease in imports while encouraging Japanese manufacturers to boost exports to make up for the drop in consumption at home, economists said.
"Car makers will continue to export unless they can raise profits from domestic sales," Yamaguchi said. In June, Japanese car exports rose 39 percent from a year earlier.
But some economists said Tokyo's trade surplus had already peaked and would gradually shrink from now on.
"The effects of the weak yen will fade and a slowing down of the U.S. economy will work to curb the trade surplus in the future," said Takao Oshita, economist at Wako Research Institute of Economics.
Oshita added that car exports were unlikely to rise any further, given the industry's fear of sparking trade friction and increased overseas production.
But Oshita said that, despite a halt in the rise of the trade surplus, a substantial drop in the current account surplus was unlikely as Japan will continue to post an income account surplus.
The income account reflects interest payments and capital gains Japanese investors receive from foreign investments.

Wako's Oshita said the income surplus was likely to continue rising in the future after reforms in Japan's foreign exchange laws are implemented in April 1998. The measure will allow freer flows of capital out of Japan, Oshita said.
The expected rise of the surplus in Japan's external balances may also put upward pressure on the yen by fuelling speculation of a flare-up in trade friction.
A strong yen makes Japanese goods more expensive in global markets, thus hurting their competitive edge and curbing exports from Japan.
In recent months, both Japanese and U.S. officials have reiterated that they have no intention of using exchange rates as a tool to correct external trade imbalances.
